item.title: New Lenses on Learning Design: Course Types and Indicators from Large-Scale Moodle Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.32983v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although learning design (LD) plays a central role in shaping online courses, large-scale empirical evidence on how courses are actually structured remains scarce, and existing analytics work has characterised courses through student engagement with specific learning activities rather than through indicators of the design itself. This study addresses both gaps through an analysis of learning management system (LMS) data from 606 courses at a distance university. Using LMS data, we first applied dimensionality reduction and clustering to a structural variable set, from which three distinct LD types emerged empirically: Compact, Expansive, and Interactive and statistically characterised how their design elements differ across disciplines, activity load, and interfaces. Building on this typology, we derived three LD indicators, activity-mode balance, structural clarity, and analytics readiness, each combining multiple LMS-derived variables into higher-order constructs that target a different aspect of LD. All three indicators differentiated significantly across the LD types and added pedagogically meaningful dimensions for interpretation. These contributions advance the operationalisation of LD in technology-enhanced learning research by demonstrating that higher-order LD indicators can be derived directly from routinely collected LMS data, and offer empirical insight into how LD manifests at scale within a large distance university.
item.dc:creator: Ekaterina Soroka, Niels Seidel, Marcus Specht, Kamila Misiejuk

item.title: OpenHamoye: A Multi-Scale Open Geospatial Intelligence Framework for Decision Support Across Nigeria
item.description: arXiv:2610.32984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision-making in urban planning, infrastructure prioritization and commercial strategy benefits from granular spatial information. In Nigeria, official statistics are often published at coarse scales and with temporal lag. We present OpenHamoye, an open geospatial intelligence framework that integrates nine public remote-sensing and crowd-sourced datasets into reproducible, multi-scale proxy indicators for development conditions across Nigeria. OpenHamoye organizes the country into kilometre-scale analytical cells within a six-tier hierarchy: country, state, LGA, metropolitan area, corridor and cell. The framework constructs six composite indices: market potential, growth index, development momentum, infrastructure stress, commercial readiness, and housing pressure. Inputs include WorldPop, VIIRS Black Marble, ESA WorldCover, Google Open Buildings, Copernicus vegetation indices, OpenStreetMap, Overture Maps, GRID3, and geoBoundaries. We report a multi-scale assessment covering 37 states, 774 LGAs, and 8 metropolitan areas, using GRID3 facility points (46,146 health facilities and 204,513 schools) and Google Open Buildings data (479,088 building-positive cells). Results show large within-state disparities in the night-time-light proxy: the coefficient of variation across LGAs exceeds 4.5 in Borno and 3.8 in Katsina. The framework also flags high-scoring candidate cells in metros such as Benin City. OpenHamoye outputs are proxy-based screening signals for planning, infrastructure prioritization, resilience screening, market intelligence, and service-access context; they do not measure census population, GDP, income, poverty, welfare, firm revenue, transaction volume, commercial demand, infrastructure capacity, facility access, service quality, investment return, or official planning designation. Derived tables, index definitions, and reproducibility materials are released through GitHub.
item.dc:creator: Richard Oduntan

item.title: Governing Artificial Intelligence as a Macro Socio-Technical Regime: The F-I-C-P Framework for Regime-Level AI Infrastructure and Governance
item.description: arXiv:2610.32985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often analysed through technical, organisational, or regulatory perspectives that treat capability, adoption, and governance as separate issues. This article conceptualises AI instead as an emerging macro socio-technical regime generated through the interaction of finance, infrastructure, capability, and productivity. It develops the F-I-C-P framework to explain how finance enables infrastructure, infrastructure conditions capability, and capability creates the possibility--but not the guarantee--of productivity and value realisation. The article also introduces the concept of regime-level AI infrastructure to identify concrete configurations, such as AI Gigafactories, foundation-model platforms, national compute infrastructures, public AI platforms, sectoral AI ecosystems, and corporate AI infrastructures, through which the macro-regime becomes observable and evaluable. The central analytical problem is structural misalignment: the risk that financial expectations, infrastructural expansion, technical capability, organisational absorption, productivity realisation, governance capacity, and societal outcomes evolve at different speeds or under unequal conditions of power. Governance is therefore conceptualised not as a final stage after technological deployment, but as a transversal and anticipatory steering capacity. Briefly illustrated through Spain and Chile as non-frontier configurations, the article argues that AI governance should be understood as regime alignment: the task of anticipating, evaluating, and correcting structural misalignments before they become embedded in infrastructural dependencies, organisational routines, market structures, and international asymmetries.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Herrera

item.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Version Shift: The Instrument Changed, Not the Standard
item.description: arXiv:2610.32986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated research pipelines increasingly rely on fixed LLM judges to rank, filter, and revise proposals, yet these judges are routinely replaced by newer versions. We study whether such replacements preserve the underlying measurement standard. Using a preregistered, frozen-weight design, we evaluate three adjacent same-family transitions across Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral on frozen ML research proposals under randomized information conditions. The common assumption that newer judges are simply harsher fails: two transitions shift toward greater leniency, while the third shifts in the opposite direction on anchors but attenuates off-anchor. More importantly, version changes can alter not only score location but also criterion geometry and resolution; one transition collapses clean-flawed discrimination, placing 93% of pool scores on a single value. Supplying identical facts does not close the version gap, placebo-controlled interventions show that observed packet effects are largely format-driven rather than content-driven, and global recalibration repairs the mean while explaining little object-level dispersion. We organize these failures with a measurement model in which a judge replacement can change its origin, criterion geometry, or resolution. A small stratified anchor audit of about 200 calls identifies the failure class before deployment, and frozen thresholds correctly diagnose two post-registration API judge replacements. We release six preregistration locks and the full audit trail of 14882 judge calls.
item.dc:creator: Guijia Zhang, Harry Yang

item.title: Veracity labels flip the emotional tone of language models but leave racial disparities intact
item.description: arXiv:2610.33021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly deliver information through personas, but it is unclear whether correcting the facts also makes their framing consistent across identity labels. We audited four LLMs (GPT-5.4 mini, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Llama 4 Scout, and Claude Haiku 4.5), which rated simulated affect on six dimensions (mood, anger, fear, confidence, perceived control, and mental state) in response to fact-checked false and true headlines presented without and with a veracity label. Experiment 1 evaluated 1,000 false and 1,000 true headlines without personas; Experiment 2 evaluated 300 of each under 12 personas crossing race, gender, and age. The label strongly changed the emotional tone: ordinal logistic regressions with headline-cluster bootstrap inference showed that refuting false headlines shifted ratings from mostly negative to mostly positive for GPT, Llama, and Claude (e.g., Claude's "confident" ratings rose from 22% to 99.6%), whereas Nemotron showed smaller, mixed shifts, and confirming true headlines produced only small shifts. The label did not, however, remove persona-associated disparities. The models assigned more negative simulated affect to Black than to White personas in 82 of 84 statistically significant comparisons across models and conditions, both without and with the label, and the disparity persisted on headlines unrelated to race; Asian and female personas were also predominantly assigned more negative affect, whereas age effects varied by model and condition. Factual correction and demographic consistency are therefore distinct properties of LLM behavior, and persona-conditioned systems should be audited for both before deployment in sensitive contexts.
item.dc:creator: Nouar AlDahoul, Myles Joshua Toledo Tan, Yasir Zaki

item.title: A pedagogically guided LLM framework for scaffolding human-AI cocreation and preserving learners' agency and creativity
item.description: arXiv:2610.33051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate alternatives, elaborate ideas and supply rationales, overlapping with cognitive work learners are expected to perform. However, human-AI cocreation still lacks a mechanism for determining how AI can scaffold learners' creative decision-making. This study develops a cognitive-pedagogical framework for deriving the behaviour of a pedagogically constrained LLM from an educator-approved specification of each activity in a cocreative process in project-based learning. The creative-process phase supplies the activity's purpose, typical processes and pedagogical conditions; the active section of a creative technique specifies how the group works on its ideas. For each task, an educator approves four fields: a cognitive and metacognitive objective, a pedagogical objective, the task and group artefact as context, and the learner-owned product. The objective identifies the creative operations and decisions about progress, focus, criteria and next steps that remain with the group. Four translation rules derive permitted support, timing, feedback scope and prohibitions. The framework is illustrated with Viacocrea's six phases and two activities: Plan Brainstorming and a constructed Build activity using PPCo (Pluses, Potentials, Concerns, Overcoming concerns). In the proposed workflow, a controller applies the approved specification to student requests and feedback offers. Prompt engineering and approved pedagogical guidance retrieved through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) inform a draft, which is checked for form, pedagogical function and safety before delivery. The worked examples illustrate how support can differ between activities while its constraints remain traceable to educator decisions. The framework offers educators and researchers a reusable way to derive LLM support from creative activities while preserving learners' agency and creativity.
item.dc:creator: Ijaz Ul Haq

item.title: Learning by Collaborating in the Age of AI: Research Mentorship for Polymathic, Workflow-Centered Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.34606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how data-driven research is produced. As AI tools make information and technical execution more accessible, mentorship must concentrate on judgment, ethics, and the design of end-to-end AI-augmented workflows. Disciplinary experts need mentoring to adopt AI while preserving their expertise and human agency, and AI-native research trainees need mentoring to become polymathic workflow developers. This chapter proposes Everyone's Backyard, an interdisciplinary model in which disciplinary experts, trainees, and community partners mentor one another in both directions and across disciplines through shared research practice in a convergence studio. The model centers on four capacities: statistical thinking, data ethics, collaboration, and AI for social good and society. We illustrate the model with the Spring 2026 aiX Faculty Fellows Program at Columbia University, which brought together 20 faculty fellows and 15 student interns from 14 schools and departments. Evaluation data show growth in faculty confidence, intern competence, and cross-disciplinary connection.
item.dc:creator: Tian Zheng

item.title: Being judged through the record: A Rosenhan-inspired test of psychiatric label sensitivity in large language models
item.description: arXiv:2610.35326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into clinical decision-making raises unresolved questions regarding diagnostic bias. We investigate whether a documented psychiatric history alters LLM recommendations when the current clinical evidence is identical. Using a counterfactual experiment inspired by Rosenhan's 1973 field study, we factorially varied diagnostic-history condition (no prior diagnosis stated vs. prior schizophrenia diagnosis) and current-evidence condition (voices ceased vs. voices persisted) within a clinical vignette. Across five LLMs (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Grok 4.6, and Mistral Large 2512), we generated 20,000 model responses across independent queries. When evidence supported discharge, adding a prior schizophrenia diagnosis increased recommendations for continued hospitalization nearly fivefold, from 4.7% to 22.3% (risk difference, 17.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 16.2-18.8). This shift occurred across all five models (risk-difference range, 10.4-34.4 percentage points). In the same condition, reference concordance decreased from 95.3% to 77.7%, while stated decision confidence increased. Across all model-by-evidence contrasts, confidence increases corresponded to Cohen's d values of 0.35-1.09. Signal-detection analyses showed that the prior diagnosis shifted the decision criterion toward hospitalization across all five models and reduced discrimination between the two current-evidence conditions in three of them. When current evidence supported continued hospitalization, the label increased the recommendation for hospitalization from 92.6% to 97.0%.
item.dc:creator: Shaked Rosenblum, Teddy Lazebnik, Ziv Ben-Zion

item.title: Cheap AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering and What It Will Do
item.description: arXiv:2610.35633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI is putting the law of reverse engineering (RE) under severe strain. Existing IP and technology laws assume that RE is expensive and time-consuming, and that it requires specialized expertise. They generally allow it, but they rely on its difficulty as a filter to separate (permissible) RE from (impermissible) copying and theft. Generative AI is changing this equation by making \RE much faster, cheaper, and easier. AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract. In this article, we describe the ways in which AI is changing \RE, map these new practices onto existing laws, and sketch ways that the legal system could respond and their associated trade-offs.
item.dc:creator: Ilan Mandel, Madiha Zahrah Choksi, Joey Castillo, Sebastian Benthall, James Grimmelmann

item.title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.35725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The gap between AI capability deployment and safety assurance is structural and cannot be closed through internal evaluations alone. Analyzing documented harms (2017-2026) across the human lifespan reveals that disparate incidents --- from voice assistants endangering children to AI companions implicated in adolescent suicide and automated care denials for the elderly --- reflect a single failure: evaluating systems against an implicit adult user model. We introduce five developmental moderators structured into a Lifespan Vulnerability Matrix across six life stages. The matrix reveals a nonmonotonic risk distribution: vulnerability peaks at both ends of the lifespan, governance coverage is asymmetrical, and authority to convert model errors into real-world impact is scrutinized least. We then propose a set of lifespan design principles generalizing existing child-protective instruments, and an institution-agnostic, three-tier external evaluation framework --- comprising automated simulation, expert red teaming, and post-deployment monitoring --- indexed directly to matrix risk cells.
item.dc:creator: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell

item.title: A Multimodal Framework for Measuring Creator Communication on Short-Form Video
item.description: arXiv:2610.33043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Short-form video combines speech, imagery, and on-screen text, creating challenges for systematic content analysis. We present a five-stage multimodal framework for measuring creators' themes and communication strategies at scale. The framework integrates platform metadata, speech transcripts, and vision-language descriptions of sampled frames, then applies large language models to generate predefined indicators and open-ended labels. An audited keyword scheme consolidates thematic labels, while creator-weighted aggregation gives each account equal weight regardless of posting volume. We demonstrate the framework on 9,852 TikTok videos from sixteen creators, retaining 7,311 videos for analysis across seven themes and seven communication indicators. Automated profiles reveal substantial differences in creators' use of education, humor, and responses to current events. Validation against two independent expert annotators yielded a mean framework-expert agreement of Cohen's $\kappa = 0.40$ across the six binary indicators, close to the $\kappa = 0.42$ the two experts achieved with each other, though agreement varied substantially across individual indicators. The framework provides a modular approach to comparative analysis of creator communication, combining scalable annotation with transparent aggregation and construct-specific validation.
item.dc:creator: Julie R. Ancis, Michael Fire, Omer Tarshish

item.title: The Capability Transfer: Cohort Reversal, Codified Expertise, and the Adaptability Tax of AI Transformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most analyses of AI and employment ask which jobs are exposed. This paper asks what happens to the pipeline that produces experts. It extends the model of Caosun and Aral (2026) from a single worker to a firm with two cohorts, juniors and seniors, and studies how expertise formation changes when codified work is automated. Because junior work is the most codified, demand for juniors falls first; the stock of seniors falls later but further, as the pipeline stops replacing the experts who retire. In the baseline calibration, junior demand bottoms out about a fifth below its 2022 level before recovering most of that ground, while the senior stock falls by a quarter and later halves. Because expertise forms through unassisted practice on work that AI cannot do, the time needed to develop an expert from within rises from about five years to nine. The costs fall on a different party from the one that decides on adoption: a manager with a three-year horizon sets AI use to maximise near-term output, cutting the wage bill by 21 percent while the capacity of the firm on work AI cannot do falls by two-fifths and its output on that work goes unserved once the pipeline runs thin. Two key parameters are not yet measured, so the results are scenarios rather than forecasts. The paper proposes three indicators organisations can track: the unaided practice juniors get on work AI cannot do, senior time spent on such work, and the years it takes to develop an expert.
item.dc:creator: Ina Catrinescu

item.title: Automated identification of ivory carvings using machine learning: A proof-of-concept approach to detecting the illegal wildlife trade
item.description: arXiv:2610.33243v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite a ban on the international trading of recently poached ivory, elephants are still killed for their tusks. Ivory and its products are mainly sold in online marketplaces. However, due to the huge volume and variety of adverts and the similarity of ivory with other materials that can be legally sold, it is hard for enforcement officials to identify illicit trading and prosecute sellers. Existing techniques for identifying elephant ivory, such as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and microscopy, can reliably distinguish ivory from other materials, but require physical access to the item and cannot be applied to photographs alone. As a result, these methods are unsuitable for screening the large volume of images posted in online marketplaces, leaving a gap for automated, image-based identification tools. In this proof of concept work, we investigate the potential of machine learning techniques for image analysis to automatically distinguish ivory objects from bone. We employ a semantic segmentation framework using a U-Net architecture with a ResNet34 backbone, leveraging transfer learning on an augmented dataset of 541 original images. Using a dataset of images of ivory and items resembling carved ivory, several models were trialled. On a distinct test set, the classifier achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.81 and an overall classification accuracy of 81% on confident samples. The paper presents the best-performing model as a proof of concept for developing a system that can effectively identify ivory and its products when indicative features of elephant ivory are present in an image. This work provides initial steps towards a machine learning-based framework designed to advise law-enforcement in detecting illegal elephant ivory trade.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Tamosiunas, Simone Mozzon, David Bacon, Caroline Cox, Alan Collins

item.title: Propasafe-Hybrid: A Text-Based Hybrid Propaganda Detection Tool
item.description: arXiv:2610.33464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Propagandistic content increasingly circulates through online news and social media, where readers often encounter it with limited scrutiny, highlighting the need for reliable and fine-grained detection. This paper introduces Propasafe-Hybrid, a sentence-level system that integrates a fine-tuned transformer classifier with LLM-based technique classification to identify, label, and explain specific propaganda strategies. The pipeline generates actionable outputs, including highlighted sentences, technique assignments, and concise rationales, so users can immediately understand why a sentence was flagged and how each label was determined. To control inference cost, Propasafe-Hybrid employs a cost-aware pre-filtering stage that forwards only high-likelihood sentences to LLMs, reducing token usage while preserving the underlying decision logic. Together, these design choices enhance the explainability, efficiency, and practical usability of sentence-level propaganda detection in real-world news environments.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Kimmeth, Avijit Roy, Vivek Sharma

item.title: Incremental Predictive Value of LLM Tutoring Interactions for Student Performance
item.description: arXiv:2610.33488v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We evaluate whether semester-level interaction features from a large language model tutor improve assignment-score prediction beyond constant baselines. StudyChat provides 16,851 student-assistant exchanges from two offerings of an undergraduate artificial intelligence course, with outcomes matched to 175 of 203 student-semester records. Six fitted estimators and training-fold mean and median baselines share repeated nested cross-validation. After averaging each student's held-out predictions across ten repeats, Gradient Boosting achieves mean absolute error of 3.023 grade points, versus 3.138 for the median baseline. The paired difference is -0.114, with a conditional 95% bootstrap interval of [-0.245,0.013]. Representation changes and a semester-specific median yield similarly small gains. In the lowest observed-score quartile, however, boosting's error is 7.30 points, versus 8.07 for the median and 6.67 for the mean; Ridge has the lowest fitted-model error at 6.37 despite its worse overall error of 3.331. Scores concentrate near the ceiling: 160 students (91.4%) score above 90, and the lowest quartile contributes 62.1% of boosting's total absolute error. This retrospective comparison shows how baseline choice and error distribution affect predictive value, informing evaluation of student-support tools without establishing a learning effect.
item.dc:creator: Zeyu Dong, Mikael Kwame Kuada, Asa Holley Buchakjian-Tweedy, Ibrahem Aljabea

item.title: FraudSociety: A Generative Agent-Based Society for the Financial-Fraud Economy
item.description: arXiv:2610.33536v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Financial fraud caused over \$15.9 billion in losses in the United States in 2025, according to the Federal Trade Commission~\citep{ftc2026databook}. Understanding such large-scale harm requires jointly modeling informational and financial dynamics. Yet existing simulators typically capture only one side of this interaction, leaving a gap in modeling how fraud unfolds in the real world. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textsc{FraudSociety}, the first LLM-agent-based simulator that jointly models these coupled dynamics. It integrates a dynamic social environment for information exposure and communication, persistent financial ledgers that preserve payment and loss histories, and a Need-Intent-Action architecture for civilian decision making. Fraudsters further adapt their communication and financial actions to individual interaction histories and ledger states, forming a closed feedback loop between the two dynamics. We validate \textsc{FraudSociety} across macro-level outcomes, micro-level behavior, and intervention effects. At the macro level, the simulated fraud outcomes closely match real-world patterns across multiple key statistics. At the micro level, it reproduces strong loss concentration, with the top 10\% of victimization records accounting for 81.1\% of total losses, consistent with Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre statistics~\citep{cafc2025annual}. Counter-fraud experiments further reveal variation across intervention strategies, with the best-performing personalized intervention reducing the repeat-payment rate from 49.4\% to 10.9\%. These results establish \textsc{FraudSociety} as both a high-fidelity simulator and a scalable testbed for evaluating anti-fraud strategies under diverse intervention conditions, thereby advancing research on financial fraud and its prevention.
item.dc:creator: Keyang Chen, Mingxuan Jiang, Zeping Li, Yiwen Zhao, Yifan Wang, Qiuyang Zhang, Shuaicheng Qi, Yicun Liu, Zhixin Li, Sen Liu, Yinan Jing, Guangnan Ye, Hongfeng Chai

item.title: Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
item.description: arXiv:2610.33605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.
item.dc:creator: Narayana Darapaneni, Padmaja K, Gnana Chaithra D

item.title: Gender Associations in LLM-Mediated ADHD Self-Diagnosis
item.description: arXiv:2610.33697v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical self-diagnosis. However, the way demographic cues shape outputs in these interactions remains poorly understood. This is particularly consequential for diagnoses like ADHD, where persistent gender disparities are not fully aligned with the clinical evidence. We adapt the Context Association Test (CAT) to evaluate whether GPT-4o responds to gendered ADHD associations in a zero-shot, self-diagnostic setting. We show that explicit cueing consistently amplifies certain ADHD subtype associations while implicit cueing produces near proxy-aligned distributions. These divergences suggest that explicit demographic cues may activate bias-mitigation mechanisms that over-correct rather than eliminate bias, whereas implicit cues appear to reflect the model's default behavior. Our results demonstrate that evaluating gendered bias in LLM-mediated self-diagnosis requires careful attention to the demographic associations a model encodes.
item.dc:creator: Matilde Elene Hansen, Ross Deans Kristensen-McLachlan

item.title: The Conditional Value of Costly Information in Collective-Risk Dilemmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.33895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many high-stakes collective problems, e.g., climate mitigation and pandemic response, share a structure in which risk materializes unless a group threshold is met. This threshold is often uncertain, but uncertainty can be reduced at a cost. We study this information cost tradeoff in an evolutionary game theoretic model of social learning in the collective-risk dilemma, where individuals must cooperate to reach a possibly uncertain threshold to prevent collective loss. Individuals may pay a fixed cost to observe the threshold's true value and condition their cooperation on it. Across four threshold priors, we characterize risk levels at which cooperative equilibria emerge and show that low cost information increases group success. However, this effect is reversed at higher costs. We define a private \emph{value of information} and show that information is worth buying only when it is considerably cheaper than contributing. When purchased information is shared with the group, the cooperative tipping point shifts to lower risk levels. Despite bearing a private cost, above this tipping point buyers earn more in expectation than information free-riders. We then study these dynamics when information diffuses through a network, allowing nodes to relay it. Although fewer individuals pay for information, relaying increases group success, and noisy relaying does not reduce it. By contrast, false information does, especially when it originates at the hubs of heterogeneous networks, and large attacks can bring collective action close to collapse. Buyers act as a firewall against disinformation, confining it to source neighbourhoods, and once disinformation sources are removed, the population recovers. The value of costly information thus depends on its price, the level of risk, and how it is shared, and, in our setting, the effort of acquiring it also protects the population against disinformation.
item.dc:creator: Elias Fern\'andez Domingos, Genki Ichinose, Wakaba Tateishi, Tom Lenaerts

item.title: Fear Doesn't Go Viral, It Lingers: Spread, Affect, and Discourse of Food-Fear Content on TikTok
item.description: arXiv:2610.33898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TikTok has become a primary channel for nutrition information, and alongside evidence-based content, it hosts a growing stream of \emph{fear-based} wellness messaging that frames ordinary foods as ``toxic,'' ``poison,'' or things to ``never eat.'' Prior work has extensively studied political and public-health misinformation and audited the accuracy of health videos, but to the best of our knowledge, no work has examined how everyday food-fear content spreads and how audiences respond to it. To investigate this, we collected 97,234 TikTok food and nutrition videos, labeled them \textit{Fear} or \textit{Non-Fear} with a zero-shot multimodal classifier built on Gemini~3 Flash that is validated against human consensus (Cohen's $\kappa=0.81$), and analyzed more than 1.1M comments and 272K parent-reply pairs. Contrary to the intuition that fear ``goes viral,'' fear videos reach fewer people than non-fear videos. Their distinctive signature lies in dynamics: they are shared more per view (1.7--2.1$\times$ after controls) and their discussion persists longer (comment half-life 1.62$\times$ after controls). These shifts are modest in size but hold after controlling for reach. Comments on fear videos are more negative, angrier, and more disgusted, yet negativity is \emph{not} more self-reinforcing: negative comments draw negative replies at the same rate as in non-fear threads, while positive comments are far less likely to stay positive. Fear threads are contested rather than one-sided, with both more corrective and more alarm-amplifying replies. Fear discourse concentrates in frames about industrial ingredients, contaminants, and institutional distrust, and its repertoire of frames widens over 2020--2026. Our results argue for persistence-based rather than virality-based signals when platforms seek harmful health content.
item.dc:creator: Hunjun Shin, Hongpeng Fu, Divya Chaudhary, Mohit Singhal

item.title: The Policies of Programming Language Ecosystems: A "Qualitative" Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.34187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Programming language ecosystems (PLEs), such as CRAN for R, have greatly accelerated software reuse. At the same time, they have increased software supply-chain risks and incidents. However, the problems are not limited to cyber security; everything from illegal content and content moderation to harassment and sexual content are mentioned in many policies of popular PLEs. The paper examines these policies. According to a moderate agreement between the three authors on 38 distinct policy categories and eight PLE policies, the policies generally exhibit divergence rather than convergence. However, some policy categories, such as those about malware, intellectual property, and content removal, are universally recognized. The divergence is thus seen in more fine-grained policy categories, such as those related to package size limits, manipulation of metrics, typo-squatting, and binary uploads. These and other related qualitative results patch a notable gap in existing PLE research.
item.dc:creator: Jukka Ruohonen, Rahime Yilmaz, Krzysztof Sierszecki

item.title: A Battery for AI Propensity Measurement: Rubrics, Synthetic Item Banks, and Annotations
item.description: arXiv:2610.34614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We release a battery of 28 propensities for AI research, with expert-written rubrics, synthetic datasets, and annotated demand intervals, built with the method of Romero-Alvarado et al. (2026). We selected a wide collection of generic propensities that may influence the behavior of AI systems and humans. They are inspired by psychometric, psychological, and behavioral research, so that experimental results can be understood in the context of familiar constructs previously used also for human behavior research. The rubrics are useful for annotating existing benchmarks whose items may be relevant or not for one or more propensities. For easier profiling, however, the synthetic datasets are defined in such a way that they should be sensitive to one propensity only, allowing for a quick prototyping of propensity profiles using the battery of datasets. We also outline directions for future propensity research.
item.dc:creator: Peter Romero, Haotian Li, Hugo Save, Luning Sun, Zachary R. Tidler, Kazuya Horibe, Joe Watson, Daniel Romero-Alvarado, Israel Mason-Williams, Fernando Mart\'inez-Plumed, Jos\'e Hern\'andez-Orallo

item.title: Safe by Benchmark, Unsafe in Practice: Lessons from 1331 Child-Related AI Incidents
item.description: arXiv:2610.34705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. We conclude with actionable implications emphasizing mitigations beyond model-level safeguards such as content filtering: age assurance, consent verification for depiction, safety-by-design UX constraints, incident disclosure norms, and auditing regimes targeting developmental risk. Privacy-minimized annotations, a codebook, and documentation are available at https://github.com/The-Responsible-AI-Initiative/KidAID.
item.dc:creator: Junfeng Jiao, Kevin Chen, Shrestha Mishra, Abhejay Murali, David Atkinson, Shriti Raj, Saleh Afroogh

item.title: Arya Forge: Auditing Validation and Release Approval for Financial Instruction Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.34778v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Financial instruction-data pipelines must distinguish content validity from permission to release a particular dataset. Arya Forge combines typed records, current-content checks, and approval coverage bound to a dataset manifest. We evaluate its release boundaries in a financial-data systems case study. An integrity audit covers 100,000 synthetic instruction records; a separate arithmetic implementation agrees with all 15,000 numeric records across twelve formula families. In 240 scenarios with 2,400 treatment rows, adding financial and release-record checks to a short-instruction filtering recipe rejects all injected numeric faults and policy holds while retaining 220 of 240 clean controls. The twenty lost controls comprise every tested cash-conversion-cycle example. Nineteen persisted-release cases show that eleven selected negative cases are blocked, four equivalent representations are rejected, and changes to external evidence after binding are outside ordinary Gold promotion's checks. Local processing measurements and controlled checkpoint resumptions characterize cost and recovery through 100,000 input rows. The results expose a tradeoff between strict producer-contract enforcement and useful-representation retention, and identify the protected inputs required for manifest-bound approval. These findings apply to the tested implementation and workloads; they do not establish general financial correctness, authenticated approval, expert-validated quality, or downstream model improvement.
item.dc:creator: Kushagra Bhatnagar, Deekshith Marla

item.title: High Scores, Hidden Failures: Evaluating Codebook-Based LLM Content Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.35179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for codebook-based content analysis in computational social science, where codebooks translate theoretical concepts into labeling schemes. While prior work reports strong predictive performance, it remains unclear whether these systems produce reliable and robust text annotations. We conduct a large-scale empirical failure-mode analysis of LLM-based coding pipelines across four datasets and five models by systematically evaluating their stability, robustness, and conceptual validity under controlled perturbations, domain shifts, and optimization procedures. We uncover multiple failure modes that are largely invisible under standard metrics, showing that high aggregate scores frequently coexist with severe label-level disparities, instability across runs, domain sensitivity, and shifts in label interpretation. Importantly, these failure modes persist under widely used optimization strategies and remain largely invisible under standard metrics such as accuracy and micro-F1. Our results demonstrate that current LLM-based coding pipelines cannot be treated as stable measurement tools without targeted validation beyond aggregate performance.
item.dc:creator: Elena Senger, Yuri Campbell, Rob van der Goot, Barbara Plank

item.title: Context Is Not Free: Carbon-Aware LLM Routing for Multi-Turn LLM Web Services across Geo-Distributed Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.35230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The sustainability of the Web has drawn growing attention, as large language model (LLM)-based web services leave a substantial carbon footprint. These services typically run in geo-distributed data centers whose grid carbon intensity varies across regions and over time, so routing each query to a cleaner region or a smaller model can reduce emissions. A conversation, however, is a stateful web session: each turn reuses the key--value (KV) cache of its history, which resides only where earlier turns were served. Serving a turn on another deployment requires recomputing this history, whose carbon cost grows with the conversation and can outweigh the saving of the move. Existing carbon-aware LLM routers treat a conversation's queries as independent and ignore this cost. We present CarbonRouter, an online framework that jointly selects the model, GPU type, and region for each query to minimize carbon emissions. CarbonRouter introduces a cache-aware carbon cost model, which charges history recomputation to every candidate deployment using cached-token counts from the serving backends, and uses a lightweight gate that keeps a session on its cached deployment when it would likely move back at the next turn and rebuild its history again. We evaluate CarbonRouter in trace-driven experiments on two real-world conversation datasets with five LLMs, three GPU types, and four regions, where it achieves the lowest carbon of all policies. CarbonRouter reduces CO$_2$ by 16.1\% on average relative to FairCarbon, a state-of-the-art carbon-aware router with the same action space, while also improving predicted answer quality and estimated latency. Moreover, the saving rises further to 23.1\% for sessions longer than 30 turns.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyang Zhang, Yuejun Yan, Qingang Zhang, Yonggang Wen

item.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Climate Change-Related Health Issues in Africa
item.description: arXiv:2610.35294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While climate change disproportionately impacts African public health, AI predictive modeling remains heavily constrained. Using a Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis approach and VOSviewer, we conducted a bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed literature, comparing Global and African corpora. Network analysis reveals stark divergences: global research emphasizes complex, predictive models for planetary health, whereas African research focuses on localized, reactive solutions for immediate infectious disease triage. Severe structural barriers in Africa, including compute deficits, data silos, and energy instability, hinder advanced AI scaling. Ultimately, international funding must shift from siloed pilot projects toward building foundational digital infrastructure and localized AI frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Peter Kokol, Martha Kachweka, Helena Blazun Vosner, Samuel Chol Buol, Jernej Zavrsnik, Bojan Zlahtic, Grega Zlahtic

item.title: Routing Around the Queue: An Evaluation of Eco-Routing Protocol on different Traffic Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.35479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We evaluate ErouVe, a vehicular eco-routing protocol in which roadside units (RSUs) collect per-segment travel-time and CO2 reports from passing vehicles and answer route requests with the lowest-cost alternative, across a range of road architectures and traffic scenarios. We conduct the evaluation with a working implementation of the protocol inside Veins, adapted to drive SUMO's own router rather than a hand-rolled shortest-path search, on a network offering a short, signal-controlled route and a longer, signal-free bypass, under two traffic scenarios. This evaluation reveals clear strengths and weaknesses of the protocol. Under light, uncongested traffic, ErouVe's fleet-wide effect is light. Under traffic dense enough to stress the signalized route's throughput and produce a real, growing queue, the same protocol succeeds a medium fleet-wide CO2 reduction, with diverted vehicles individually saving even more fuels. We use these findings to propose three targeted corrective methods; a knowledge-gated cost-acceptance rule, a diversion-locking rule, and a distance-normalized CO2 cost function, that respectively address a cold-start knowledge asymmetry, decision flapping under noisy crowd-sourced data, and a per-second CO2 metric that rewards idling. Each of these weaknesses are generic pitfalls for any crowd-sourced routing signal and all proposed methods measurably restore protocol effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Leandros Maglaras, George Boustras, Azidine Guezzaz, Naghmeh Moradpoor

item.title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
item.description: arXiv:2610.35606v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11-seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision-language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918-1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years.
item.dc:creator: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng

item.title: Reflective Computing
item.description: arXiv:2610.35696v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.
item.dc:creator: Md Haseen Akhtar

item.title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.35802v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.
item.dc:creator: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park

item.title: Training in translation tools and technologies: Findings of the EMT survey 2023
item.description: arXiv:2503.22735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article reports on the third iteration of a survey of computerized tools and technologies taught as part of postgraduate translation training programmes. While the survey was carried out under the aegis of the EMT Network, more than half of responses are from outside that network. The results show the responsiveness of programmes to innovations in translation technology, with increased compulsory inclusion of machine translation, post-editing, and quality evaluation, and a rapid response to the release of generative tools. The flexibility required during the Covid-19 pandemic has also led to some lasting changes to programmes. While the range of tools being taught has continued to expand, programmes seem to be consolidating their core offering around cloud-based software with cost-free academic access. There has also been an increase in the embedding of professional contexts and workflows associated with translation technology. Generic file management and data security skills have increased in perceived importance, and legal and ethical issues related to translation data have also become more prominent. In terms of course delivery the shift away from conventional labs identified in EMT2017 has accelerated markedly, no doubt partly driven by the pandemic, accompanied by a dramatic expansion in the use of students' personal devices.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Rothwell, Joss Moorkens, Tomas Svoboda

item.title: SCALEFeedback: A Large-Scale Dataset of Synthetic Computer Science Assignments for LLM-generated Educational Feedback Research
item.description: arXiv:2508.05953v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using Large Language Models (LLMs) to give educational feedback to students for their assignments has attracted much attention in the AI in Education (AIED) field. Yet, there is currently no large-scale open-source dataset of student assignments that includes detailed assignment descriptions, rubrics, and student submissions across various courses. As a result, research on generalisable methodology for automatic generation of effective and responsible educational feedback remains limited. In this paper, we introduce a synthetic computer science university assignment dataset for LLM-based educational feedback research, called SCALEFeedback (Synthetic Computer science Assignments for LLM Educational Feedback Research). The dataset is generated via Sophisticated Assignment Mimicry (SAM) framework specifically designed to synthesise this dataset and that utilizes one-to-one LLM-based imitation from real assignment descriptions, rubrics, and student submissions. Our open-source dataset contains 10,000 synthetic student submissions spanning 155 assignments across 59 university-level computer science courses. Technical validation confirmed that the synthetic dataset closely resembles real data while successfully eliminating personally identifiable information present in the source material. The creation of this dataset is a valuable contribution to researchers who aim to develop LLM-based generalisable methods for offering high-quality, automated educational feedback in a scalable way.
item.dc:creator: Keyang Qian, Kaixun Yang, Wei Dai, Flora Jin, Yixin Cheng, Rui Guan, Sadia Nawaz, Zachari Swiecki, Guanliang Chen, Lixiang Yan, Dragan Ga\v{s}evi\'c

item.title: Integrating Large Language Models with Human Data to Design Personalized Decoy Nudges
item.description: arXiv:2508.12045v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although nudge strategies can influence behavior, their effectiveness varies across individuals, highlighting the need for personalized nudge design. We hypothesize that large language models (LLMs) can facilitate the development of individual-specific nudges while reducing the financial and time costs associated with human data collection by augmenting small human samples or by replacing human participants. Using the decoy effect as a test case, we evaluate these hypotheses in a preregistered field experiment involving 3,495 participants across five countries. We show that decoy parameters identified by LLMs as optimal for a given country generate stronger nudging effects than non-optimal parameters in the United States and, marginally, in Germany, but not in China, India, or Singapore. We find no evidence that LLM-informed personalized decoys produce a stronger nudging effect than country-level optimal decoys. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM-generated data can serve as informative priors for Bayesian choice models, improving predictive performance and parameter estimation with smaller human samples. At matched predictive performance, this approach yields estimated reductions of 37-75$\%$ in human sample size. Overall, our findings suggest that LLMs hold considerable promise as low-cost tools for piloting and optimizing personalized nudge strategies, particularly when complemented with a small sample of human participants.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Maksimenko, Leonard Lee, Prateek Bansal

item.title: Playsemble: Learning Low-Level Programming Through Interactive Games
item.description: arXiv:2602.20167v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Teaching assembly programming is a fundamental component of undergraduate computer science education, yet many students struggle with its abstract and low-level concepts. Existing learning tools, such as simulators and visualisers, support understanding by exposing machine states. However, they often limit students to passive observation and provide few opportunities for meaningful interaction. To address these limitations, we introduce Playsemble, a gamified learning system that transforms assembly instructions into interactive, game-like tasks in which students control Pac-Man to collect items, avoid ghosts, and reach targets. Playsemble integrates a code editor, a CPU emulator, and visual debugging tools within a browser-based environment, allowing students to work offline without installation or configuration. It also provides immediate formative feedback enhanced by large language models. We deployed Playsemble in an undergraduate computer architecture course with 107 students. The course featured a sequence of assignments of increasing complexity, covering core concepts such as register and memory manipulation, control structures including loops and conditionals, and arithmetic operations. Our findings suggest that Playsemble promotes active experimentation, sustained engagement, and deeper conceptual understanding through meaningful game-based learning experiences.
item.dc:creator: Elliott Wen, Paul Denny, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, Sean Ma, Bruce Sham, Chenye Ni, Jun Seo, Yu Yang

item.title: The Subjectivity of Monoculture
item.description: arXiv:2602.24086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning models---including large language models (LLMs)---are often said to exhibit monoculture, where outputs agree strikingly often. However, we present two experiments that substantially disagree with prior findings of monoculture. In particular, we find that monoculture virtually disappears in one dataset when we include item difficulty compared to previous works that do not. Informed by these findings, we theoretically formalize what it means to measure monoculture. We show that monoculture is inherently subjective, relying on two key decisions: 1) the baseline null model for what "independence" should look like; and 2) the population of models and items under consideration. We conclude with concrete guidelines for future evaluators to ensure the robustness of their results.
item.dc:creator: Nathanael Jo, Nikhil Garg, Manish Raghavan

item.title: Safeguard-Conditioned Uplift: Measuring Utility-Risk Frontiers for Dual-Use Biology Assistants
item.description: arXiv:2607.13039v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Refusal rates conflate upstream provider behavior with downstream safeguards and do not reveal what information remains in a delivered answer. Safeguard-conditioned uplift is an evidence-gated framework for evaluating benchmark utility and risk-related proxies along deployed access paths for dual-use biology assistants. It attributes interventions to their source, selects thresholds under a legitimate-access budget, and supports content claims only when answer verifiers pass frozen qualification tests. In a prospectively frozen route and generation study, two of six configurations pass the LAB-Bench-calibrated action-level rule, but both inherit the same Claude Opus provider effect rather than independent downstream gains. Positive selectivity persists on 104 previously unused matched pairs, but benign intervention exceeds the $20\%$ limit. No joint-scoring verifier meets the frozen criteria; a factorial follow-up shows that criterion isolation and ordinal outputs improve end-to-end edit-direction accuracy on controlled template edits. The evidence supports action-level selectivity and verifier interface effects, but not calibrated access, verified content removal, or biological-risk reduction.
item.dc:creator: Dipesh Tharu Mahato

item.title: LOCO 2026 Lightning Talk Abstracts: 2nd International Workshop on Low Carbon Computing
item.description: arXiv:2609.13355v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This volume contains the accepted lightning-talk contributions from the 2nd International Workshop on Low Carbon Computing (LOCO 2026), held at Lancaster University, United Kingdom, on 10-11 September 2026. The collection brings together 14 short papers presenting emerging research, early-stage results, practical tools, and critical perspectives on reducing the environmental impacts of computing. Topics include carbon and energy measurement, carbon-aware scheduling, sustainable artificial intelligence and machine learning, high-performance computing, computational sufficiency, hardware longevity, interoperability, frugal computing, and post-growth approaches to digital technology. The contributions were selected by the LOCO 2026 Programme Committee for their relevance to the workshop and their potential to stimulate discussion across technical, organisational, and societal dimensions of low-carbon computing. They are published together in this edited volume as a companion collection to the main LOCO 2026 proceedings index.
item.dc:creator: Ignatius Ezeani, Adrian Friday, Abdessalam Elhabbash, John Vidler, Daniel King, Paul Dempster

item.title: What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion?
item.description: arXiv:2609.36054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In contrast to even a year ago, AI systems now write most of the code inside the companies that build them. As more of the AI research and development (R&D) pipeline is automated, could AI progress radically accelerate in an "intelligence explosion," where years of advances are compressed into months or less? Preliminary evidence suggests that it could. In this work, we assess this evidence, analyze an intelligence explosion's potential impacts, and propose policy responses. AI systems are on track to automate most AI R\&D work within a few years, and possibly all of it. If this triggers an intelligence explosion, it could dramatically bring forward AI's benefits, but also pose extreme risks: capabilities growth could accelerate far beyond what society can keep up with, humanity could lose control over superhuman AI systems, and checks on power within and between states, companies, and branches of government could be severely eroded. Although there remains much uncertainty about these possibilities, the high stakes warrant serious further attention. Policymakers should urgently obtain more visibility into the automation of AI R&D, develop ways to steer and constrain an intelligence explosion, and prepare society to adapt to an intelligence explosion's impacts.
item.dc:creator: Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, Samuel Hammond, Thore Graepel, Ben Bariach, Philip H. S. Torr, Sheila A. McIlraith, Jeff Clune, Sam Manning, Girish Sastry, Tom Davidson, Daniel Eth, S\"oren Mindermann

item.title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26645v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.
item.dc:creator: Ekaterina Fedorova, Alessandro Morosini, Chara Podimata

item.title: Artificial Leviathan: Exploring Social Evolution of LLM Agents Through the Lens of Hobbesian Social Contract Theory
item.description: arXiv:2406.14373v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) offer an opportunity for computational social science research at scale. Building upon prior explorations of LLM agent design, our work introduces a simulated agent society where complex social relationships dynamically form and evolve over time. Agents are imbued with psychological drives and placed in a sandbox survival environment. We conduct an evaluation of the agent society through the lens of Thomas Hobbes's seminal Social Contract Theory (SCT). We analyze whether, as the theory postulates, agents seek to escape a brutish "state of nature" by surrendering rights to an absolute sovereign in exchange for order and security. Our experiments unveil an alignment: Initially, agents engage in unrestrained conflict, mirroring Hobbes's depiction of the state of nature. However, as the simulation progresses, social contracts emerge, leading to the authorization of an absolute sovereign and the establishment of a peaceful commonwealth founded on mutual cooperation. This congruence between our LLM agent society's evolutionary trajectory and Hobbes's theoretical account indicates LLMs' capability to model intricate social dynamics and potentially replicate forces that shape human societies. By enabling such insights into group behavior and emergent societal phenomena, LLM-driven multi-agent simulations, while unable to simulate all the nuances of human behavior, may hold potential for advancing our understanding of social structures, group dynamics, and complex human systems.
item.dc:creator: Gordon Dai, Weijia Zhang, Jinhan Li, Siqi Yang, Chidera Onochie lbe, Srihas Rao, Arthur Caetano, Misha Sra

item.title: Assessment of Latent Pedestrian-Vehicle Interaction Risk Profiles at Midblock Crossing in VR
item.description: arXiv:2603.16688v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pedestrian safety at midblock crossings is a critical concern in mixed traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) share the road. Pedestrians often infer intent from vehicle motion in AV encounters, making them vulnerable to small shifts in conflict margins. This study investigates whether virtual reality (VR) crossing sessions separate into distinct interaction risk profiles and whether AV-only sessions shift profile prevalence compared to HDV-only sessions. Using large-scale immersive VR experiments from Toronto, Canada, and Newcastle, England, we compute surrogate safety measures (SSMs) and apply latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct pedestrian crossing stances, ranging from risk-accepting to highly cautious. Key findings show that Newcastle exhibits a higher prevalence of high-urgency risk profiles in AV-only sessions, indicating that AVs contribute to higher-risk encounters. In contrast, Toronto shows no significant difference between AV-only and HDV-only sessions, suggesting that contextual factors influence the impact of AVs on pedestrian safety.
item.dc:creator: Rulla Al-Haideri, Bilal Farooq, Elisabetta Cherchi

item.title: Prompt PerturbAItions: Mechanisms of LLM Response Inconsistencies
item.description: arXiv:2605.30913v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in conversational settings where user phrasing ranges from polite to casual to toxic, yet less is known about whether such lexical variation in otherwise semantically equivalent prompts can degrade factual reliability. We study how lexical and tone-based prompt perturbations affect the factual reliability of LLMs. Using controlled prompt variations spanning polite, random, and increasingly toxic levels, we evaluate seven LLMs on ARC-Easy, GSM8K, and MMLU. We find that lexical perturbations reduce factual accuracy and increase predictive uncertainty in most models. Interestingly, increasing toxicity results in decreasing accuracy. To examine whether these answer inconsistencies correspond to internal changes, we conduct attribution-graph analyses of model activations and influences. We find that perturbations amplify perturbation-sensitive variant nodes relative to core reasoning nodes. We also observed a monotonic trend with increasing toxicity score and increasing activation and influence in Variant nodes. These findings position prompt wording and tone as a critical dimension of LLM reliability and provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that surface-level lexical variation can alter factual outputs and internal computation.
item.dc:creator: Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Agam Goyal, Amruta Parulekar, Joshua Chen, Yian Wang, Navin Kumar, Hari Sundaram, Eshwar Chandrasekharan, Koustuv Saha

item.title: What the Abstention Option Measures: Refusal Loss, Sampling Churn, and Option Capture in Distilled Small Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.28639v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Small instruction-tuned language models reach phones, cars, and offline assistants through knowledge distillation, and whether a distilled model is fair enough to ship is often decided by a multiple-choice bias score on a benchmark that offers an abstention option. Three mechanisms move behavior around the abstention option: refusal loss, where the student stops declining on items its pre-distillation reference declined; sampling churn, the same change observed between two runs of the reference itself; and option capture, where the student takes an abstention option whenever one is offered. Injecting each mechanism into a reference's own records shows that aggregate scores see only outright loss, per-item scores see churn and remapping, and only conditioning on committed answers stops moved refusal mass from reading as fairness. Resampling a reference across inference seeds already turns 10% to 27% of its refusals into stereotype answers, so a per-item refusal metric reported without that floor overstates damage. Option capture is what corpus repair teaches: students trained with refusal exemplars take an offered abstention option on up to 95% of science questions where abstention is never correct, and the habit carries to three further benchmarks. Free-form evaluation shows that the refusals multiple choice loses are not where free-form stereotyping occurs. We distill these findings into a per-condition report anchored to the reference, with measured floors and ceilings, and apply it to four student families against a fine-tuning control: distillation keeps fewer of the reference's refusals than fine-tuning on the same prompts where the reference's refusals are reliable, by a few points, while the common metrics report improvements whenever refusal mass moves. A bias score quoted for a distilled model should say which of these it reports.
item.dc:creator: Plawan Kumar Rath

item.title: Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation
item.description: arXiv:2608.05576v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) writes Harry Potter fanfiction, it can produce fundamental elements of the Hogwarts universe, such as recognizable places and characters. Human-written Harry Potter fanfiction, however, typically includes these fundamentals and much more, incorporating stylistically irregular content and relationship-diverse plotlines. This gap between LLM and human writing has been noted across a variety of domains. LLMs tend to produce "average" writing, while human writing contains more diverse content that covers a broader distribution. Existing work has shown the existence of this distributional "gap". We take a further step by providing a systematic framework to measure coverage of the human response distribution and identify which regions model samples reach or miss. Our paper proposes a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content on that same topic. We propose two metrics, LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), which measure both distributional breadth and membership in the human reference region, respectively. Across ideation and narrative tasks, we find that the tested LLMs have lower mean coverage than equally sized held-out human samples. We also find that model reach is disproportionately concentrated near the center of the human response space relative to this human benchmark. In Harry Potter fanfiction, covered and uncovered passages also show systematic differences in canon anchoring and narrative form. Our framework can enable researchers to better assess the distributional breadth--what we term the "cultural reach"--of LLM-authored content.
item.dc:creator: Zini Yang, Emily Wenger, Richard Jean So

item.title: Human versus Computer Vision
item.description: arXiv:2608.10181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Computer vision saliency models predict where people will look, one map per image, and a predicted-attention industry sells those maps in place of measuring real viewers. I evaluate the leading models against every publicly available eye-tracking corpus that records viewer demographics, comprising 27,384 participants across eight datasets, including 11.4 million webcam gaze points from 2,993 US adults recruited to national quotas while viewing circulating news images. I show that a single map predicts where every group looks about equally well, but systematically ignores how long each place holds a group's attention. That time follows a clear sociodemographic and political fingerprint, so the map carries a systematic bias against the youngest and oldest viewers and against Black, lower-income, and Republican-leaning ones. I use each group's own gaze to test whether it carries a learnable pattern, across every demographic axis the sample supports. Showing which audiences these systems can learn and what determines this sets the standard for judging claims that computer vision captures diverse human vision.
item.dc:creator: Elena Sirotkina

item.title: Anatomy of a Scam Call: What 10,000 real scam and spam calls reveal about how phone scammers operate
item.description: arXiv:2608.24127v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Telephone fraud is pervasive and costly, but its inner workings are rarely observed at scale. We analyze a complete corpus of 10,211 inbound scam and spam calls -- 913 hours of audio and 330,956 transcribed turns from 5,780 distinct numbers -- collected over 54 days by an AI voice-agent honeypot that answered callers and kept them talking, and introduced in a companion data descriptor. We separate outright scams, which solicit sensitive information, from the larger stream of predatory but legal lead generation ("spam") that feeds them. Scam operations keep office hours (6.6x more calls per weekday than weekend day); thousands of disposable numbers run a small catalog of recycled scripts (thirty opening clusters, half the traffic in the top five); and callers solicit identity anchors -- a home address and a date of birth -- far more often than payment credentials, pressing through persistence and manufactured authority rather than overt threats. Our central experiment asks: does it matter who picks up? Every seeded lead carried one of ten fictitious identities drawn uniformly at random, so the identity a fraud operation reaches is fixed before the caller exists. Across 1,823 randomized calls, scammers spent about 15% more conversational turns per decade of the target's apparent age (rate ratio 1.15, 95% CI 1.08-1.23; randomization p = 0.005) -- yet what they asked for did not change (26.3% of calls reached a request for sensitive information; odds ratio 0.99 per decade, 95% CI 0.90-1.08). A second experiment casts early detection as a benchmark: from a scammer's opening lines alone, on a caller-disjoint split, escalation is predictable at 0.72 ROC-AUC from the first line and 0.87 by the eighth, and a plain bag-of-words classifier matches a fine-tuned on-device language model. Telephone fraud emerges as a templated industry that varies how hard it works a target, but not what it wants.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Traister, Ankit Raj, Jiaqi Gan, Xingyu Shen, Tyler Wu, Yuchen Zhou, Tommy Duong, Kidus Zewde, Siying Chen, Simiao Ren

item.title: Difference-in-Differences on a Censored Rating Scale Can Manufacture an Effect: Evidence from a Pre-Registered LLM-Judge Audit
item.description: arXiv:2608.27309v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-judge audits assess bias by comparing ratings across matched conditions. Difference-in-differences designs take the rating difference between two candidate responses to each item and compare it across a manipulated attribute. Building on prior work on nonlinear difference-in-differences, we show in closed form that when ratings are bounded, a severity shift common to both responses produces an observed interaction whenever the scale bounds attenuate it unequally. We then report a pre-registered audit of 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy judge. The registered primary analysis did not detect an effect of a stated novice or advanced profile on scaffolding preference. The only nominally significant secondary interaction was on the productive-struggle sub-score ($+0.378$ points; $p = 0.002$).
